content: Bathybious haeckelii was a substance initially believed by British biologist Thomas Henry Huxley to represent a form of primordial matter, potentially the origin of all organic life. However, Huxley later acknowledged that this interpretation was incorrect, as the substance was ultimately determined to be a product of a chemical reaction. In 1868, Huxley examined a preserved sample of mud from the Atlantic seafloor, originally collected in 1857. When first analyzed, the sample contained only protozoan cells, and Huxley had stored it in alcohol for preservation. Upon re-examination, he observed an albuminous slime with vein-like structures. Convinced he had discovered a new organic substance, he named it Bathybious haeckelii in honor of German philosopher Ernst Haeckel, who had theorized about Urschleim (primordial slime), a protoplasm from which all life might have originated. Huxley speculated that Bathybious could be this protoplasm, a potential link between inorganic matter and organic life. He published his findings and informed Haeckel, who was impressed and obtained a sample for himself. In the next edition of his textbook, The History of Creation, Haeckel suggested that the substance was continuously forming at the bottom of the sea. Huxley disagreed but hypothesized that Bathybious might form a continuous mat of living protoplasm across the ocean floor. Other scientists were skeptical. In 1869, Charles Wyville Thomson examined samples and likened them to fungal mycelium, while George Charles Wallich argued that Bathybious was merely a product of chemical disintegration. The Challenger expedition, which began in 1872 and lasted three years, collected 363 samples from the ocean floor but found no evidence of Bathybious, despite claims of its supposed ubiquity. In 1875, John Young Buchanan, the ship's chemist, analyzed a substance resembling Bathybious and determined it to be a precipitate of calcium sulfate formed by the reaction of seawater with the preservative alcohol. Buchanan suspected that all Bathybious samples had been similarly produced and informed Thomson, the expedition leader. Thomson, in turn, wrote to Huxley about the findings. Realizing his error, Huxley published part of Thomson's letter in Nature and retracted his earlier claims. During the 1879 meeting of the British Association for the Advancement of Science, Huxley took full responsibility for propagating the theory and convincing others of its validity. Most biologists accepted his acknowledgment of the mistake. However, Haeckel, whose theories about Urschleim were closely tied to the idea of Bathybious, was reluctant to abandon the concept. He continued to assert, without evidence, that Bathybious had been observed in the Atlantic and maintained this position until 1883. Huxley's rival, George Charles Wallich, accused him of deliberate fraud and also accused Haeckel of falsifying data. Haeckel had indeed created a series of illustrations depicting the evolution of Urschleim, which he claimed were based on observations. Opponents of evolution, including the Duke of Argyll and modern creationists, have since used the Bathybious case as an argument against evolutionary theory.
